lede: Open a Bunsen's air hole and the flame is small, blue and clean. Close it and the same gas burns yellow and smoky and blackens everything. How much oxygen a fuel gets decides what comes out of it, and what that does once it is out.
can: Write balanced equations for complete and incomplete combustion.
Test for carbon dioxide and water and state the results in full.
Give the three pollution routes the specification lists.

text: Complete and incomplete combustion, and pollution from fuels

md: Open the air hole on a Bunsen burner and the flame goes small, blue and fierce. Close it and the flame turns large, yellow and smoky, and leaves black marks on anything held in it. Same gas, same burner: what changed is how much oxygen it is getting.

prompt: In the picture above, which burner is getting plenty of oxygen?
options: the one with the air hole open
the one with the air hole closed
answer: the one with the air hole open
explain: The open air hole lets plenty of oxygen in, which is what makes the flame clean and leaves no soot.

caption: One carbon and four hydrogens: only two elements can come out of it.

md:
With **plenty of oxygen**, a hydrocarbon burns completely and gives **carbon dioxide** and **water**:
methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, or $\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$.
When a question asks for the **formulae** of the products, write $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$. Examiners report the names being written instead, and names earn nothing when formulae were asked for.

title: Why those two products and no others
md: A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen, so those are the only two elements that can end up in the products. Each carbon takes oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide; each pair of hydrogens takes oxygen and becomes water. Nothing else is available to make anything else from.

prompt: Methane burns completely in plenty of oxygen. Which pair gives the formulae of the products?
explain: Formulae were asked for, so CO₂ and H₂O. The names are right chemistry but the wrong form of answer, and CO belongs to incomplete combustion.

md:
Two tests, and both need their result stated in full.
**Water**: it condenses in the cooled U-tube as a colourless liquid. Add **anhydrous copper(II) sulfate** and it turns from **white to blue**.
**Carbon dioxide**: **bubble the gas through limewater** and the **colourless** solution **turns milky**. Say *colourless*, not *clear*: examiners refuse *clear* every year.

prompt: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater. The colourless solution turns ______.
explain: Milky. Name the starting colour too: the scheme wants colourless to milky, and 'clear' is not accepted for colourless.

caption: The smoky flame on the right is short of oxygen.

md: With a **limited supply of oxygen** the fuel cannot burn completely. The products are **carbon monoxide** and **water**, and **sometimes carbon** as well, seen as **soot**. CCEA does not ask for an equation that makes soot, but it does ask for one that makes carbon monoxide: $\ce{2CH4 + 3O2 -> 2CO + 4H2O}$.

prompt: Methane burns in a limited supply of oxygen. Name the toxic gas produced.
explain: Carbon monoxide. It is the product that makes a badly serviced boiler dangerous, and it is worth a mark on its own.

text: 4. Worked example: balancing a combustion equation

alt: A table counting the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms on each side of the equation for burning methane.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 620 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cac"><title id="cac">A table counting the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms on each side of a combustion equation</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3"><path d="M40 60 H580"/><path d="M40 100 H580"/><path d="M40 220 H580"/><path d="M40 60 V220"/><path d="M150 60 V220"/><path d="M360 60 V220"/><path d="M580 60 V220"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="currentColor"><text x="56" y="86" font-weight="600">Atom</text><text x="166" y="86" font-weight="600">On the left</text><text x="376" y="86" font-weight="600">On the right</text><text x="56" y="128">C</text><text x="166" y="128">1</text><text x="376" y="128">1</text><text x="56" y="166">H</text><text x="166" y="166">4</text><text x="376" y="166">4</text><text x="56" y="204">O</text><text x="166" y="204">4</text><text x="376" y="204">1 × 2 + 2 = 4</text><text x="40" y="30" font-size="13" font-weight="600">CH₄ + 2O₂ → 1CO₂ + 2H₂O</text><text x="40" y="46" font-size="11.5">Carbons first, hydrogens second, oxygen last, because oxygen sits in both products.</text></g></svg>
caption: The count that settles the balancing, side by side.

md:
**The question.** Propane, $\ce{C3H8}$, burns completely in oxygen. Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction. **[3]**
**Step 1 — write the products first.** Complete combustion always gives $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$.
**Step 2 — balance the carbons, then the hydrogens.** Three carbons need **3** $\ce{CO2}$; eight hydrogens need **4** $\ce{H2O}$.

prompt: Continue step 2. Propane, C₃H₈, has eight hydrogen atoms. How many molecules of H₂O do those hydrogens make?
explain: Four: each water molecule takes two hydrogens, and 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Carbons first, hydrogens second, oxygen last.

md:
**Step 3 — count the oxygen atoms on the right, and balance last.** 3 × 2 from the carbon dioxide plus 4 × 1 from the water is 10 oxygen atoms, which is 5 molecules of $\ce{O2}$.
**The finished equation.** $\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$. Oxygen is balanced last **because it appears in both products**, so its count is only fixed once they are.

prompt: Balance the complete combustion of methane the same way: CH₄ + ___ O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. What number goes in the gap?
explain: 2. The products hold 2 + 2 = 4 oxygen atoms, and each O₂ molecule brings two of them.

md: Three routes, and the specification names all three. **Carbon dioxide** from any hydrocarbon adds to the **greenhouse effect**, causing **climate change, sea-level rise and flooding**. **Carbon monoxide** is **toxic** and **soot** particles **damage the lungs**. **Sulfur impurities** in the fuel burn to give sulfur dioxide, which causes **acid rain**: it **damages buildings, destroys vegetation and kills fish**.

title: Why carbon monoxide is dangerous
md: It **combines with haemoglobin** in the blood, the molecule that normally carries oxygen round the body. Once carbon monoxide is attached, that haemoglobin cannot pick oxygen up, so the blood's **capacity to carry oxygen is reduced**. The gas is colourless and has no smell, so there is nothing to warn you.

options: it combines with haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen
it dissolves in water in the lungs to make an acid
answer: it combines with haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen
explain: Haemoglobin is the word the scheme wants, with what that does: the blood's capacity to carry oxygen is reduced.

title: One thing in the video below CCEA does not examine
md: Other boards add the **oxides of nitrogen** made when the air itself gets hot enough inside an engine. CCEA's Double Award specification lists only carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and soot, and the sulfur dioxide that comes from sulfur impurities, so a nitrogen-oxide answer earns nothing here.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Pollutants from Fuels"
why: A second run through the pollutants and what each one does.

prompt: Which pollutant from burning fuels causes acid rain?
options: sulfur dioxide, from sulfur impurities in the fuel
answer: sulfur dioxide, from sulfur impurities in the fuel
explain: Sulfur dioxide. Carbon dioxide's problem is the greenhouse effect, and soot's is the lungs; keep the three routes apart.

md:
write the word and symbol equations for **complete** combustion, and give the products as **formulae**.
write the equation for **incomplete** combustion, and name **carbon monoxide** and **soot**.
give the test for **water** (white to blue) and for **carbon dioxide** (colourless limewater to milky).
say why carbon monoxide is toxic, using the word **haemoglobin**.
give the three pollution routes: carbon dioxide and the greenhouse effect, carbon monoxide and soot, and sulfur dioxide and acid rain.

This sits in Question 4 of the C2 paper. The first mark is usually a product named or written as a formula; the last is a balanced equation. Stuck on the balancing? Carbons first, then hydrogens, then oxygen last. The Sheet below lists the traps.
